name: wxhtzdy ORO Tree
description: After (finally) qualifying for the IOI 2023, wxhtzdy was very happy, so he decided to do what most competitive programmers do: trying to guess the problems that will be on IOI. During this process, he accidentally made a problem, which he thought was really cool. You are given a tree (a connected acyclic graph) with $$$n$$$ vertices and $$$n-1$$$ edges. Vertex $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le n$$$) has a value $$$a_i$$$. Lets' define $$$g(u, v)$$$ as the bitwise or of the values of all vertices on the shortest path from $$$u$$$ to $$$v$$$. For example, let's say that we want to calculate $$$g(3, 4)$$$, on the tree from the first test case in the example. On the path from $$$3$$$ to $$$4$$$ are vertices $$$3$$$, $$$1$$$, $$$4$$$. Then, $$$g(3, 4) = a_3 \ | \ a_1 \ | \ a_4$$$ (here, $$$|$$$ represents the bitwise OR operation ). Also, you are given $$$q$$$ queries, and each query looks like this: You are given $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$. Let's consider all vertices $$$z$$$ such that $$$z$$$ is on the shortest path from $$$x$$$ to $$$y$$$ (inclusive). Lets define the niceness of a vertex $$$z$$$ as the sum of the number of non-zero bits in $$$g(x, z)$$$ and the number of non-zero bits in $$$g(y, z)$$$. You need to find the maximum niceness among all vertices $$$z$$$ on the shortest path from $$$x$$$ to $$$y$$$. Since his brain is really tired after solving an output only problem on SIO (he had to do it to qualify for the IOI), he wants your help with this problem.
input_specification: The first line of input contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of vertices. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ positive integers $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_v \le 10^9$$$) — the value of each vertex, the $$$i$$$-th integer in this line corresponds to the vertex $$$i$$$. Following $$$n - 1$$$ lines are the description of a tree. Each line contains two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n, u \ne v$$$) — indicating that vertices $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ are connected by an edge. The next line contains a single integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 10^5$$$) — number of queries. Following $$$q$$$ lines contain 2 integers $$$x, y$$$ ($$$1 \le x, y \le n$$$) — the vertices $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$ for each query. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$q$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case output $$$q$$$ integers, each of which is the answer to the corresponding query.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1878G — wxhtzdy ORO Tree [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
